newsitem.title: USA: NYC gays seek to be part of Irish parade.
newsitem.headline: NYC gays seek to be part of Irish parade.

text.p: A group of Irish-American gays and lesbians, in what has become a rite of spring in New York, on Thursday called on organizers of the 236th annual St. Patrick's Day parade to let them march together in the traditional event.
The group has been rebuffed for several years in its efforts to join Monday's parade to celebrate Ireland's national holiday.

Organizers of the New York event -- a Roman Catholic group called the Ancient Order of Hibernians -- have long refused to let the gays and lesbians march because the church believes homosexuality is wrong.

"Make this St. Patrick's Day parade an inclusive one, and one which all Irish-Americans and all New Yorkers can be proud of and participate in," said City Councilman Tom Duane at a news conference with the Irish Lesbian and Gay Organization (ILGO) on the steps of City Hall.
Members of the group vowed to live up to their protest chant of "We're Irish. We're queer. We'll be here every year."
"Those people who wish we would go away, well, they're just out of luck," said ILGO member John Francis Mulligan.

Democratic mayoral contenders Rev. Al Sharpton, Manhattan Borough President Ruth Messinger and Bronx Borough President Fernando Ferrer have said they would not march in the parade if the group were excluded.
Republican Mayor Rudolph Giuliani has marched in years past and aides say he will be in the parade again this year.
Representatives for the parade organizers were not available for comment after the gay group's news conference, but they have indicated they would not change their position.
The parade traditionally features thousands of bagpipers, high school bands and a sea of uniformed police who march up Fifth Avenue. More than a million people attend each year.
The gay group first applied to participate in 1991.

In previous years, the group has held protests before the parade and dozens of members have been arrested on disorderly conduct charges. The group said it was still deciding what action, if any, to take this year.
Its efforts were dealt a setback in 1995, when the Supreme Court ruled that organizers of a St. Patrick's Day parade in Boston had the constitutional free-speech right to exclude gays and lesbians.

ILGO has filed lawsuits against the New York City Police Department, which has denied it permits to hold its own march on the same day as the parade. The department has argued two parades would strain city services and cause congestion.
While the issue is controversial in New York, gays freely march in St. Patrick's Day parades in Ireland.
